Roy Eldridge (6/15/82 & 6/22/83): These dates are correct
Now, Roy, you were born in Pittsburgh in 1911, January 31st?
No, 30th.
January 30, 1911. Did your family always live in Pittsburgh? Or did your parents come from others parts of the country?

Well, no. My father came from North Carolina. Actually, he was born in Virginia, but I can't think of the name of the town. Not Alexandria, somewhere else. Petersburg, I think it was. And my mother was born in North Carolina, you know. But he was raised in North Carolina, my father, I would say, yeah. But me, I was born in Pittsburgh! -- heh-heh.
And you had an older brother.
Yeah, I had a brother. Two brothers and a sister. And I think there were... So I understand, there was twelve of us, and I'm the last of the crop!
You were the youngest.
Yeah.
Now, I know that your brother Joe was musical. Was there anybody else who played in the family?
My mother played piano. I think that's where I got mine from, was her. Because when I was little, around five or six years old, I got a set of drums, of toy drums
Eldridge - 2

for Christmas. And we used to go to the theatre, and in the theatre they always had the piano player that used to play for the movies, and she would come home and play these things that she'd heard. She wouldn't need no music or nothing, because she could them, you know. And I would play the drums with her, you know. So I think that's where the ear comes from, you know, being able to hear things.

Of course, Joe was a different thing. He went and studied violin, and he studied harmony and arranging, and saxophone, you know. So it was a different story with him. Plus, I never had too much eyes for being a musician in the first place!
What did you want to be?

Well, my father, you know... Like, the first I remember him as a kid, he used to have horses. He was in the transport business, you know. Then he got into the contracting business, and this goes way back when T-models was in style, you know. We had one T-model, a Sunday T-model, and it had a brass rail -- it was a touring car, you know. And me and Joe used to have to shine it every Sunday, and clean the car. And he had about three or four trucks that he used to haul machinery and stuff like that. And with me, that's what I wanted to do, drive one of the trucks, you know.
Eldridge - 3

Then as time progressed, he ended up with bigger trucks, you know. And I'll never forget, I used to... He had, I can't think of the name of it, I think it was a Haynes(?) or something, and I could get that one started by cranking it. And I would crank it as far as I could get it, out the garage and into the wall!
How old were you at that time?
I guess about 10 or 11 years old, you know. Yeah, it's funny how you... I loved those cars!
The story goes that you played your first professional engagement on drums on New Year's Eve when you were very, very young.

I think I was six years old at the date. It was my brother, he played violin. And Tatum, not Art Tatum (what's the cat's name?)...Clarence Tatum is his name... He played piano and the other Tatum played French horn. And we had French horn, drums, piano, violin, and Norman Sampson played the clarinet. It was on New Year's Eve. And when twelve o'clock come, I was noddin'!...heh-heh-heh... It was a pretty wild party.
Was it a private party?
Yeah, it was a private party at somebody's house. There were people running around naked and all that shit. Heh-heh.
Eldridge - 4

But that still didn't make me want to get into music. You know, it was more fun out playing in the streets, you know. And my father tried to interest me in business. In other words, he had a lot of real estate and he had... See, the railroad track used to be down...the Pennsylvania Railroad, where they used to switch the trains. And he had this rooming house outside of the rail station, and the guys that worked on the railroad used to stay upstairs, you know. Then there was a barber-shop next to that. So he had a little space in there between that, and then he bought us... We had a shoeshine stand. We also had the equipment to clean hats, you know. Just trying to get a start in the business, you know. And that lasted awhile until Joe went away, and then it went by the boards. And I stayed there a little while, but I wasn't good at it. Joe was but I wasn't, you know. So that folded up.

And I took a little piano lessons. But what happened was that the piano player, the teacher was one of those mean cats, you know. And he'd always be slapping my hands and things like that, you know, and I didn't dig that. Plus, when you get to look like (?). This guy used to put (?) on his hair so it would stand ...(?)... And it was pretty frightening. So I didn't spend the money. I saved the money and backed out, and told my parents that I couldn't...
Eldridge - 5
I wasn't making it with the teacher.
Then I took drum lessons for a while with Mr. Catlett. He was the best drummer around there as far as band drumming was concerned, you know.
Catlett. He wasn't related to Sid, was he?

No. I don't think so, no. So my brother knew I was getting stuck on the drums, and he didn't want me to go that route, because he said, 'One thing, you're not going to get too big' and... We were talking about this last night. The drums in those days were like 28 inches, you know. Sometimes bigger. And carrying all those drums, with the big tom-toms and the cymbals, it would be too much! And you didn't have no band-boys in those days, you know.
So he talked my people into getting me a horn for Christmas. They got me a trumpet. And I started taking lessons off P.M. Williams.
How do you spell that first name?

Just P.M. Like night, nighttime. But he had played on circuses and carnivals and things like that, and he had some helluva chops, man -- Jesus. If I had listened to him, I would have been really a powerful trumpet player, a legitimate trumpet player, because he... You know, they had them marches. You could hear this cat twenty blocks away, above everybody, you know. He had them good chops,
Eldridge - 6

you know. But my only fault was that I listened to him, but he made the mistake of playing the lesson before I played it. And when he would do that, if I heard it I could play it, you know. And he thought I was reading it. I wasn't reading that.
You picked everything up by ear.

Yeah! Once he played it, I had it, you know. And I'll never forget the first time we played out. We played in church. And he was worried to death because we had a duet to play. And I was talkin' to some of my buddies. He said, "Sit up there and look at your music," you know. It didn't make any difference, I didn't know what it was anyhow, you know. But when the thing came, it went off like clockwork.

Then I joined a drum-and-bugle corps. And that I really enjoyed, because I couldn't wait until the parades, like Decoration Day. Because I would get up like six o'clock in the morning and go out on the roof over our garage, and get my snare drum and tune it up, and boy, I'm telling you... When you get at the end of the night, those drums are still beating in your ears. But that's a good feeling, you know, marching in front of all these people.
Then one time... Oh, I think this is before I started playing trumpet. They got short of buglers, and so they
Eldridge - 7

just handed me a bugle. That's right. That's before I started playing trumpet. And I could play it. I just picked it up and played it. Except for one thing, something that hasn't left me in all these years, is being nervous when I had to play. Because the first time we played... It had nothing to do with it being in the graveyard. It was just that like all my buddies from my side of town (we lived on the north side) was... See, what they did was, they stationed each bugler at a certain distance from the graveyard, you know. And when they'd play Taps...[SINGS FIRST FEW BARS OF 'TAPS']...and you're supposed to pick that up. If it had been the second one, I don't think I would have been nervous to this day. But like, they went there, and they went there, and they went there, and they went there, and it looked like I was the last one. And when it got to me, I was in a cold sweat. I said, "No, oh, whoo-hoo..." Heh-heh. So I sounded like a nanny goat! And that's something that stuck with ever since then, you know.

Of course, I'd been on the stage before that. I was in a stage play with... Save the life of me, I can't figure out what the heck the play was. It was at one of the theatres downtown. And a bunch of us kids, like, naturally shootin' crap...heh-heh. What else, huh!? Then the lady come in who
Eldridge - 8
was supposed to be our mother, and we all ran to her, you know.
Was it a school performance?

No, no, it was regular legit theatre. Yeah. Then my brother, he came back home... No, before they left to go to New York. That's right. They used to rehearse at our house. And I used to put them down, because... And I think I was right, too -- although I didn't know I was right then. What they used to do, they'd... Well, they'd shake up the neighborhood, of course. It was a hell of a band. Eli Sarnees(?) (?) with the band once, and also Benny Carter. And they'd rehearse over a couple of numbers, and then they'd play one of their shouts, you know -- really tear the neighborhood up. Then the food. My mother had food for them, and big pots full, and these cats would eat like dogs, man. I told my mother, "(?)'s coming over to play because of that food!" Heh-heh.
So that band went to New York?
Yeah, they went to New York. Yeah, they went.... Joe stayed in New York. He came home once, man, and he had his coat(?) ...(?)...(?)...(?)...(?)...
You were still not sure that you wanted to be a musician?
No, by this time... It had gotten to me by
Eldridge - 9

then. Because I... We just...a couple of other little cats I knew, we were playing around, you know. We'd be taking things off the records, like Red Nichols. Because I wasn't exposed to Louis Armstrong then, you know. Or Bix. It was Rex then, and Red Nichols, you know.

Well, actually, what got me started was the trumpet player that was in my brother's band, a ...(?)... named Archie Johnson. He was a killer, man, you know. Then Rex came and stayed at our house, and he showed me a couple of breaks. Man, he was really my idol. I mean, like I couldn't... I didn't dig it because I didn't get fat like he was, you know, so I could look like him. I started to do everything he did, you know. When he came in with Fletcher, he got me and took me, and he set behind me and he's showing what he's reading and all these parts, you know. And all his mannerisms that he was... It was for me, you know.

But really the one that instilled the thing about being competitive and wanting to cut people was Horace Henderson. I give that cat all the credit in the world. I never mentioned that, but he needs some credit. Because he brought me in his band, and I told him, 'I can't read.' He says, 'You'll be all right,' you know. And I played third, and somehow or other, I could come up with the third part, you know.
Eldridge - 10

He used to tell me all these wonderful stories about New York, you know. How you walk in the bar, the nightclub or something, and the guy is sitting over in the corner in overalls and things, and you think you're playing real great, and this cat will get up and, heh-heh, stretch and have a little drink of wine, and reach in this paper brown sack, pull out his trumpet, start on low G, and when he stops, man, he's up to high G, you know, above C. That was a high note then, in those days.
Mmm-hmm.

And it's a funny thing. That story stuck with me all those years, because when I first came to New York I would always look around before I played, to see if I could see anybody acting like they were sleeping. In fact, to tell the truth, I played that trick on some trumpet players myself, heh-heh, in the Thirties. Like I was too drunk to play, you know. They'd jump all over me, then I'd wake up and [POUNDS HAND] [LAUGHS HEARTILY]
Well, before you went with Horace Henderson, a few other things happened to you. Right?

Oh yeah. We used to play for basketball(?) games... Chuck Jefferson, he was around here for a while -- he died last year. He ...(?).... And I think that's when we really got into it, because we was hangin' out late, and
Eldridge - 11

we started smokin' cigarettes, you know, sneakin' a little taste and everything like that. We'd go to Homestead and play these different house parties and things, and pick us up some money, you know. Then we got the job to go...
This is when I left to school. Got a job to go to Sharon, Pennsylvania, with this road show, you know. In the meantime, I got kicked out of school. I told you that...
No. For what?

Well, there was this little girl, ha... It was a White girl, you know. And right from babies we'd been tight, you know. We'd never really got into it, but we started getting close, you know. And it was getting to that stage where it was about to jump off. Man, we got caught in the cloakroom in the wrong position, you know. So they expelled both of us. But we were supposed to go back. And the date my father was supposed to come from work and take me back, that's the morning I left home. ]

And we got out... The first crack out the box, we got stranded. We got through... Well, to start off with... This is the funniest thing about that gig. We were rehearsing, rehearsing tunes and all that, and then when we got there, they had music. But the music was like the music where... It ain't like they do today, you know. If the spit comes out of the valve it destroyed the manuscript. That don't
Eldridge - 12
happen today; it just runs off. It was all smeared up. And even if I could read, I'd have had trouble, you know!

I think that the opening number was "What Are The Melons(?) Like In Dixie." [LAUGHS, SINGS] A (?) thing. So the cat says... We had time to rehearse. The curtain is down. "Okay, hit it!" And the curtain went up, and all five of us started crying because none of us could read. So he yells, "What the hell is the matter!?" I'm the one that spoke out and said, "We can't read no music." "Oh my God!", you know. So they figured out a tune that we could play, so they could use it for the opening, and they did that, you know. Then the comedian came on. And we played for the dancer, a one-legged dancer, Fox. Then the singer. And we got through the show, you know.
Was it a five-piece band?
We had a five-piece band, yeah. Let's see now, was it five? We had a banjo, piano, Chuck, myself (three), Charlie(?) leaves four, and something else has to leave five... Did I say banjo?
Yes.
Oh, Alvin Burroughs on drums.
No kidding.
Yeah. And that was it, man. We got out that night, went back to our pad. The lady at the pad locked our
Eldridge - 13

things up; you know, we couldn't get in our room. And it was one of those times where the only kind of work you could do this (?), which is about two miles from Sharon, is to work in the steel mill, you know. So what we did, we rented a... Well, the one-legged dancer, Fox was his name, he rented a storefront and rented a piano, and we used to give shows -- just ten cents to get in. And would you believe it? Man, the people would stand outside and dig the show, and wouldn't spend ten cents to come in and see it. It was pitiful, man. But we did go out in the daytime, and then you'd get some money, so we got some food -- you know, we were all eating there. Oh, it was a rough time, man.

Then we finally got a gig. Some guy wanted the band to go to Youngstown to play a dance, you know. And the money was nice. I guess it must have been about five dollars each. That was nice then, you know. Heh... He said, "Do you fellows want anything to eat before you go?" So the cats said, "Yeah, we'll have a sandwich or something." So we ate big hot dogs and we got bottles of Lehigh soda (back then they called them "pop" I think), and I had me three of those big hot dogs and two bottles of Lehigh. And when we get to the gig, I'm so full, I can't hit a note! All night I was fixing my valves, you know... But we got paid.
Then we got hooked up with another show there that was
Eldridge - 14

playing, like, Youngstown and some other little town close by. You know, you leave towns close enough to (?). That's where I got my good gig. I hooked up with this chick, man; we were supposed to be married, I guess. And she was a (?) on a carnival. Well, (?) we hooked up with her. And she was going with the guy that owned the hotel. And they were giving a party for these people on the carnival. So she had asked us to play for it. Well, naturally, man, we had been playing. And all these musicians there, 42(?) pieces... They had us play "Stampede," and had me play Coleman Hawkins' chorus on "Stampede." Now, that's way back in the Twenties, right? And they said, "I don't believe this. I don't believe this kid, man!" -- and right away, they gave me a job.

But they still didn't know I couldn't read. And they didn't know I'd never played outdoors! I had a (?) little old pea-shooter that had never been cleaned out, you know. They had bought this arrangement on "Stampede" and was playing oom-pah behind me, you know, and it was so loud you couldn't hear me! The only way I'd get ...(?)... was like playing the singers. But the piano players didn't like that. The singers liked for me to play behind them, you know. But the piano players: "Put that goddamn horn down!" They used to embarrass me (?), and all night long in the
Eldridge - 15
Pullman cars they'd be playing cards and talking about me. "Won't never be nothin'," you know, like that. And I hadn't been there twelve hours when they said I had my hand in the man's pocket.

There were some funny things happened. Like, they finally tricked me, the first trumpet player... They found out I couldn't read. Because I was playing all them marches and classical tunes that they played, but by ear, you know. So the first trumpet player purposely stayed on. We were trapped in the Pullman car, and he stayed in there after (?). Cat said, "Eldridge, you take this part." Cat had five trumpets. Why give it to me? But that was to psych me out, to see whether I could read or not, you know. And I'll never forget the piece. It was "Hello, Room(?)", with those intervals. And nobody had played it! See, if they had played any parts of it, I could have got started, you know.

So he tapped, he said, "Okay, hit it now," and he gives the downbeat, and no first trumpet. "Let's try it again." So I still was trying to fake it. I said, "I think somebody's not reading their part right." He said, "Well, you play your part..." [LAUGHS] That's where they got me, you know. So then I was really in bad shape around them. Until the drummer left, or they couldn't find the drummer, and I could play the show. I was playing marches and
Eldridge - 16
Classical music. That's when I ended up playing drums for them. Same twelve dollars.
Where did the show travel to?
All through Canada. All over. All over Canada and through the Midwest, you know. Then we came down back South. We hit...

Well, the first time I really knew about this prejudice thing is when we got to Cumberland, Maryland. And I seen something happen there that really shook me up, you know. We was playing a prayer date. And this Black guy had his stand like right here, you know, and when we come in, they put the ropes up on one side of his stand, like on these seats for that part of the stage you know. So the guy just asked him, 'Would you move, just move... You're blocking the seats here.' So man, they went into their thing, you know. So the next thing you know, there was a little light scuffle, you know. The guy that owned the show, Captain John Sheesley, he come, and he hit the cat in the head with his cane.

So the policeman was signalling to us. See, I figured the policeman would stop it, you know. The policeman took the Black cats to jail. ....[INAUDIBLE TWO SENTENCES].... And that night I was on the train right back to Pittsburgh.
So at that time, I had the reputation that I was a good
Eldridge - 17
trumpet player, but I wouldn't stay nowhere. Because any time the money got strange or some of this stuff... But this thing... I got back on...

Oh, I went on another show. I came back home, and I went on a show called Rock Dinah. That's when I had my own band. That's when I met Liz(?) Face(?). We travelled all over, including the South, you know, and I was featured on there. That's where I got cut, one of these chicks that got me the job on the carnival. She was on the show...
She was an entertainer?
Yes.
Was she a singer?

She was a singer-dancer. Boy, she split my back wide open. Whew. With a razor blade. And I was a fool. You see, it wouldn't have been so bad if it had been in New York or somewhere like that, because instead of taking me to the hospital, the cat sewed me up and then they put her behind bars, but with 26 stitches in my back that's why... Looking like something happened in space(?), you know.

When I got out, the judge...everybody... I heard about things that she was doing that I didn't even dream, you know. Man, I was just fifteen. Yeah, I'd just turned fifteen. And oh, they told me so many things, I hated them
Eldridge - 18

all, you know. But it was all true. Because I hadn't known, but I found out, you know. And the judge said, "Well, how much time do you want her to have?" I said, "Oh, turn her loose. I love her." He said, "You're a damn fool. Thirty days!" Well, see, that thirty days strands her, you know, because we'd be long gone. So I used to get these pleading letters, you know... She wanted to come back, and I said, "No way."

And I stayed with that thing until... Oh, we had some real evil experiences with that. We went down there... Let's see, where did we go first? We went down to Oklahoma...no, Missouri. You used to have meal tickets, you know. And I was always one to devise some way to get what I needed. And I had one of those cartons like you put ice cream in, you know. I used to keep it. Because I've always been a slow eater, you know. Cats, man, come with a boarding house reach; and there is one, believe me!
So, like, I was kind of raised a little proper, and... I always feel a draft when I hear the noise out there, because somebody stole a car out there -- just today!
I would eat slow, and every time I'd look around, everything is...
[PAUSE/CHECK MACHINE]
We were talking about meal tickets.
Eldridge - 19

Yeah. There was a place called Kroger, Kansas, and that's when I finally got hip, you know. Because one of the older guys on the show told me, "Man, you can't sit there acting cute, waiting for somebody to pass you something. You got to reach and grab!" And the thing about it, you had that meal, and you had your breakfast and your supper -- then I used to always get hungry late at night. And there was never nothin', no restaurants or nothin' in those days, you know. Of course, you had no money to go there anyhow, you know, if there had've been.

So I devised this way with this box. And the first thing I'd do is, I'd fill my plate up, and before I ate any of the food, then I'd fill my box up, like, with biscuits and whatever the meat and whatever vegetables I had. You know, just load that full up, and then I had that for later and put the top on it. And then I'd go on and eat!
Those were some bad days, man.
You were the bandleader on that tour?

Yeah. They changed my name, naturally. They've been doing that since time began. If you're the leader of something, you have to have a different name. Your name don't fit, you know. So they called me Roy Elliott and His Palais Royal Orchestra of New York.
Yeah, I used to... We had a nice little band. We had
Eldridge - 20

no bass. My feature was "East St. Louis Toodle-O." I used to have a tin can painted gold, and I used to do like the camel walk, like what they called the camel walk, coming down and playing that O-OHH-DU... I never could growl, but I did it some kind of way, you know. Heh-heh.
So you were listening to Duke then?
No! Except that I had heard, you know. My band was Fletcher's band. That was my band. And Red Nichols' Five Pennies; I liked them.
But that has surprised some people when you've mentioned that. But I guess those records were pretty hip at that time.

Well, I liked them, because those were what I was exposed to. It's a funny thing. The first time Lips Page heard me, he said, "Goddamn, where did this cat come from playing like an ofay, man?" But I was playing like Bix, you know! Things like that. And plus, playing like a saxophone, which put me away from the trumpet, with the split notes and the Louis Armstrong scene, you know, that... So it was a little strange to hear me!
You said you met Lips pretty early.
Yeah, we were in Oklahoma City, playing, of all the theatres, the Eldridge Theatre -- the name of the theatre. I think he was with the Blue Devils then. Yeah, I
Eldridge - 21
think he was with the Blue Devils.
And I guess he was on a Louis kick then, wasn't he?

To me, I called it a Southern trumpet player. The way some of those guys played like that, to me, was like Southern trumpet playing, really because... Well I had never heard nobody play like that, you know. And by that time, I had heard the distinction between the North and the South.

It's a funny thing about that. I come from a time that was very prejudiced. Of course, I didn't realize it. Oh, we were all in school together, you know, living next to each other in the same integrated neighborhoods. But, like, the theatres... You couldn't go to sit anywhere in the theatre you wanted, you know. We had like the last six rows for Negroes, you know. So we had all of that going. And...
[PAUSE]

No, it's like in the theatres over in town there, you had to sit in the balcony. But you didn't pay that any attention, you know. But when you'd get out there, you were really seeing what was really happening in the world, boy, it's scary, you know. Pshew!
Yeah, man, let's see... Oklahoma City and then we went to... Oh, we had this little road show, too; you know, this was a road show. And I'll never forget, man. We had... Do
Eldridge - 22
you remember Bergie(?) Hines? She was a vocalist.
Yeah, only.... She's just a name to me.
You never heard her sing, did you?
Oh yeah, on a record, I think.

Yeah, she was a good singer. She must have been related to Earl at one time, wasn't she? I think so. Well, her uncle and aunt was the one that had this show, Rock Dinah (?), that I was on when we went down there. And they had a number by a guy named Johnny Bagsley(?), who wore his hair slick, straight, you know, and they were doing various... He wore.... This number, "If I Could Be With You One Hour Tonight." And he had the smoking jacket on, and she had the negligee on, and they had this screen up between them when they were talking on the phone...

By the way, this was... See, we played like in a pit(?) one part of the night, and then the next part we went to a place called "Trees". That's enough time to get from one theatre to the other and set up, you know. And what they did to keep us from playing in the pit, everybody came with either a bucket of ashes or water, so we couldn't sit in the pit, you know. You awake?
Yeah!
Oh, that was mean there. Then this number
Eldridge - 23

that he did, you know, 'This Sounds So Good, I Don't Know What To Do'... Really like a movie type of thing, right? Man, the cat said, 'Hey, forget that. Put a clean dress on her and put him in some overalls, and put some black on his face.' They wouldn't go for him being dressed up like that, you know, and her being dressed up like...
What part of the country was that?
Oklahoma. Pritchard, Oklahoma. Trees. Oh, it was a drag. When I think of that shit that happened down there.

And I was also there after that show broke up... See, we left... When we got from the South there, we come to Kansas City, and we played at the Eighteenth Street Theatre. That's when Basie stole my saxophone player and my banjo player. Because Basie was with Gonzelle White then, you know. I looked up, and he got both of them and gone!
Who were they?

Hildred Humphries and... I forget the big old banjo player's name; I don't think he ever amounted to anything. Hildred was doing all right for a while, but he's in some kind of other business. He lives upstate there somewhere. Do you know Frank Humphries?
Yeah, sure.
It's his brother!
Eldridge - 24
So Basie stole him, huh?
Yeah! With Gonzelle White... He was with Gonzelle White, you know.
How did they do that? Would they come up to a guy and say, "Hey, come with us and you'll make more money" and so on?

But you see what happened, I should have been making money way back there. They got "Drumboogie" out for me, and I had a tune called "We Open," which was made when Gene recorded, "It's That Drummer's Band." That was like his theme song. Now, you realize all the residuals that I'd have got off of that if they had really...I mean, royalties, if they had given me what I was supposed to get, you know. "How About That Mess(?)", that was another one.
Was that yours too?
Yeah. Oh, there was about five or six tunes that I did that have been recorded, and he got a lot of play out of them, you know.
Anyhow, Gene wanted me to... He wanted to put me through school, you know, just to arrange -- learn how to arrange, you know... But you know, that ain't my style. I
Eldridge - 124
like to play too much.

So things kind of petered out in Chicago, and I went to New York to see Glaser... Because I had an apartment there, on Michigan Boulevard...not Michigan, on 55th -- 55th and Michigan. When I went back to New York, then I got Waverly(?) to come back with me... No, I went to see Glaser. I called him up and said, "I'm coming in." He said, "Well, be at my office at ten o'clock." When I got there at ten o'clock, he'd gone to Chicago.

So in the meantime, Gene had asked me about joining the band. Well, this is before... No, when I came back, he asked me. So I said, "Well, I'm going to go to Chicago, and I want to close up my apartment anyhow." So Waverly went with me, and then we went there, and then I got all my shit together and I... He was supposed to be at the Congress Hotel. Every time I'd call him, he just went out, you know.
Glaser?
Yeah. So finally they said, "Oh, he's gone back to New York." And I left word that I was going to be there! So I went back to New York and called him.
In the meantime, I had been in touch with Frank Vernier(?), and they were talking about me going with Gene. But I know...off the turnpike...
Charlie Barnet.
Eldridge - 125

Charlie Barnet had tried to get me, and Joe Glaser asked him for ten thousand dollars for my contract. But he was scared of that. I don't blame him, you know. So they knew that. So I had given them the information. So when I went down there to see what he had for me, he started saying, "Well, I can put you in this club here." I said, "Look, I can get those things myself." I said, "You know what? I'm tired of having a band? I've been offered to go with several bands, and I think I might try one of them bands." He said, "What you got in mind?" I said, "Well..." He said, "Well, whoever gets you, if they want to buy your contract, it's okay with me." So I said, "Well, I was thinking about Gene Krupa; I might get on as band-boy or something." He said, "Did you talk to him?" I said, "No, I'm going to go down and talk to him." That day they were rehearsing; they were opening up at the Pennsylvania Hotel. He said, "Well, if they want to buy your contract, okay." I said, "Well, I've got to know what to tell them how much it is." He said, "Well, if they give me a thousand dollars..." I said, "Well, they're going to take it out of my salary." "Well, they've got to sign something to say they'll take so much out each week, and send to me."
So I went to the White Rose, and I called him up, and he said, "Well, just hang out a while and don't go back up
Eldridge - 126

there." So I stayed there and drank a while, and drank and drank, made a couple of other spots. Then I called, and he says, "Okay, go up there and tell them that... The manager will be up to talk to you. I don't know about taking the money out of you, how that works out, but Frank will work it out.
So what happened was, Frank went up there...
To Joe?

To Joe, yeah. He went up to Joe, and he asked Joe if... And Joe told Frank he wanted a thousand dollars for the thing, but he had to sign something that he would take so much out of my pay each week to pay for it. So Frank said, "Okay. But I want to take the contract with me -- and you'll get your money." He signed the thing, and Frank's got the contract -- and the secretary snatched that thing out of his hand. He's still got that same secretary up there; she still works in the office, I think -- Miss Church. Frank snatched it back, and she snatched it back, and he said, "Well, no deal. I want to take the contract with me." So he finally got the contract, you know.
So then they called me. I called back down there, and they said "Everything's straight."
So that's how I got with the band. But I wasn't working in the band, as a member of the band. It was just a
Eldridge - 127
night(?). But that worked out all right. The first date I played with them... Oh, I have to backtrack on this.

What happened was that I went and played one of those (?) gigs in Providence. That's what happened. And when I came back, they wanted to make the deal. I was a little ahead of myself, you know. So in respect, that goes back here. I played those three dates in Providence, and then when they decided on me joining the band as a permanent thing, like an act in it. Like Teddy and Lionel were. They were an act, you know, when they first got in the band.

So that transpired. So they went in the Pennsylvania Hotel, and I opened up there with him. And everything was going along fine. But at the end they used to play this finale; they used to play "One O'Clock Jump." And I used to have to share that seat with Shorty Sherock -- which he turned out to be a great buddy of mine after he got out of the band. But he reneged, man. He said, "Man, I'm not gonna... The cat's taking my solo and I got to share my chair with him, too!" So they got into a beef about it, so they let him go.

It was a funny band. Because I can read anything. And I got in the band, people used to come to me: "What are you doing what that book in front of you? You know you can't read no music." They'd be surprised, heh-heh. Intelligent
Eldridge - 128
people! But I made it and everything.
Even Gene's wife, she said... I told them, 'Well, I'll have a book.' She says, 'You must be kidding.' I said, 'No, I ain't kidding.' Hell, I turned out to be the big thing for the band, you know.

I had one little incident there. We was playing 'Rockin' Chair'... Benny Carter had worked with them over at Meadowbrook, had made an arrangement on 'Rockin' Chair.' You know, Benny didn't know until he talked to me last year that he didn't make that arrangement for me? He thought that he had made that arrangement for me, and he made it for himself! But the way I did...my doing it and him doing it was two different things, you know.

So we were playing this thing, and it was... This is before I was sitting in the band I think this happened. Two ladies sitting down, old ladies sitting down in front of the band, they were eating this soup or something like that, and he called this 'Rockin' Chair.' And I couldn't say no. So the minute I walked out to play, they dropped this bowl, and said(?), 'Oh Christ. Because this Black dude, I know damn well he gonna blow us out of the joint.' I just had the feeling, because I could look at their disgust when I walked out, you know. Seeing me, the only Black face up there, you know.
Eldridge - 129

So I got into the piece and everything. And so, when it got around there at the end, the band was high(?) and I had to play to get above the band. So I did that, and man, they were... I thought they were gonna have a fit. So I tried to hit the note on the end soft, and I split that fella in a million damn pieces! Well, I was embarrassed! And that always ....[MOTOR NOISE]...., that "Rockin' Chair." That's the reason when I made it, I was blind drunk.
The record.
Yeah. I don't know I could have got through it if I had been sober. I still had that thing on me from that hotel, you know.
Did you play that every night, "Rockin' Chair"?

No, that's the thing. I didn't play it every night. We probably played it at the wrong time, you know. Like, he pulled that on me once in the Palladium. We had a battle of music against Harry James. And that was a funny thing, man. All the things I had to play, he played nothing that I had to play all night long -- until the broadcast came. And way down in the broadcast, he's got "Rockin' Chair." And I had played very little Jazz all night long, which was rare for me, you know. In other words, it was like he would just set me aside for the night, you know. And I'm telling you, I went in training for that thing. For
Eldridge - 130
two weeks I didn't drink, I didn't smoke, and I practiced every day, and I was ready for it, you know. But this here takes all the fun(?) out of it, you know.

But shit, things don't work out like that for people. They try, but it just don't work out. So what happened was that when he finally called this thing, man, I'd say the first two or three bars I was nervous as a dog, then all of a sudden, just something took a hold of me, and I just forgot about the crowd, the band and everything, and I played it. And I got to the end and I thought about them two old ladies, and I hit the F note, and it looked it was going to split -- and I screamed the loudest A you ever seen in your life. I just refused to let that thing go down there, you know. And I got a standing ovation.

So Gene tried to go into his next number. Couldn't make it. I had to play an encore. And he hated that, you know. So then he played "After You've Gone". It reminded me of Zutty. [SINGS OLD-TIMEY TEMPO] I mean, come on!
So where we at now?
We're still with Gene. So everybody was okay in the band? You didn't have any problems with...
With the guys?
With the guys.
Well, no. There was only two guys that I
Eldridge - 131
really dug in the band, I mean, as far as being straight on the black-and-white thing, was Ray Biondi and Graham Young, really. But the rest of the cats was... No.
And Gene was... You were pretty tight before you joined the band.

Well, we'd got tight from making that thing, you know, "Swing Is Here." That was my tune, too, and they jumped in on that. In fact, there's a melody floating around... I think I made a record with that melody in France, called "Leila Doll" or something like that. Because Spud Murphy... Do you remember Spud Murphy? You've heard of him, right?
Sure.

Well, they wanted the melody to this thing. See, first of all, I wouldn't do it because I knew what was going to happen. So Spud kept on asking me about this new chord, you know, to just help me (?) the thing out. So I wrote out the melody and the chords and everything, and carried it down to Robbins(?). And within a year's time, I went in and asked him, "What about...? You didn't send no contract." "For what?" I said, "For 'Swing Is Here'." "That's Benny Goodman's tune. You ain't got nothin' to do with that tune." I said, "Benny Goodman? Get out of here!" So the cat that was managing me... Sam Beers! That's who it
Eldridge - 132
was. He said he'd sue them if they put it out, you know. And that's why I never come out with that melody.
Yes, it's a long road, man. A long, hard road.
I meant to ask you, in between, before you went with Gene, wasn't there a brief time where you stopped playing and you studied radio engineering or something?
Oh yeah. Oh, I was doing that, yeah. That was before I went with Glaser. You're right. That was just before I went with Joe. You're right.
What caused you to do that.

Well, I always did dig it. I just started to get into it, and got books and wires and shit upstairs. Then the... Well, you see, the thing about it, when I get started in something like that, all of a sudden I don't have enough money to sustain it, and I have to go out and work. Once you get out there working and traveling, you can't get into the thing, you know. I've got some tools downstairs that I bought, and I don't even know how to use them! I forgot how to use them, you know.

So it was just something that I always liked. And really, I should have done it years ago and really finished it, and I'd have been straight now. But you know how... With musicians, it seems feast or famine. For a while you're doin' great, and then you... See, I never was a cat
Eldridge - 133

to throw away nothin', but I just had to live. Even when I wasn't steady... I mean working under ...(?)..., there was times I'd be working and there was times I wouldn't be working, you know. Then when you're not working, you've still got to live. Rent goes on, food goes on. Before you know it, you're wiped out. You got to start taking them gigs listening with the phone.
Yeah, I would have to have finished that. I still would... I started again, a different course.
Did you go to school then, at that time?

No, I was taking a correspondence course -- and getting good marks. I started the same thing again, doing... Well, I got sick this time; that's why I stopped. It's a shame, as long as I've been up, I should have been working. I don't know, I just didn't have that get-up for it. And everything's obsolete now, you know. Like, I used to take the radio. I got tube-checkers, testers and all that. They don't have them things!
That's ancient history now.

They got little chips in there... I took one of them things apart, I was gonna fix it. I said, 'Oh no!' There's not that much stuff in there. Yeah, it's a different show now. And it's gonna get different than that.
Sure. They keep inventing new things. Now they've got
Eldridge - 134
the digital stuff.
Have you got one of those computers yet?
No, but I'm thinking about getting one.
I'm going to wait until they get a little cheaper.
Oh, they will.
Oh, you know why. Everybody's getting in on the scene. Texas, they lost a lot of money.
They lost a lot.
I heard that ...(?)... was doing the commercial. But it's not his fault, though. But I'll bet he gets blamed for it.
Oh, I don't think so.
Sure they will!
They just over-extended themselves, I guess.

Well, it's not only that. There's just so many of them. Do you realize how many different companies are out there with those word processors and computers? There's too many of them. That's why i say now they're down to... You can get a whole one for about a hundred dollars now, can't you?
Yeah, that's the little ones. But then you have to buy a lot of additional stuff.
Yeah. Then the software, what they call it,
Eldridge - 135
right? Franz Jackson, he got him one. He said, 'Man, this is really a lot of fun.' But you really got to study to learn how to work them.
Oh, speaking of people... When you were with Gene, did you more or less discover Charlie Ventura? You found him, didn't you? Or you talked them into...

Well, what happened was that I used to go to a place and play, and he used to play down there, you know. And I told Gene about him, and he got the job in the band. But then he was going to leave. Because you know, when you go in a band, they don't give you nothin' to do, and he was getting disgusted. And I'm the one that kept him there, otherwise he would have been back in Philadelphia years ago.
He was working in the shipyards or something?
Yeah. Man, he's gone to pot, too, now. I seen him in Florida.
How long ago was that?
Oh, it must have been about... When I worked down in Fort Lauderdale.
Because somebody told me that he's much better now. He met a nice lady and moved to California, and he's in much better shape. She's taking good care of him.
He's in California now?
Yeah.
Eldridge - 136
You sure?
That's what I heard.
Uh-huh. Man, I just talked to somebody who said he was still in Florida. He was down there repairing instruments.
Well, I don't remember who told me this, but it was not long ago. It was maybe a few months ago.
This is in Fort Lauderdale. Well, maybe so. That was in 1980, when I seen him.
Yeah, according to what I heard, this lady had a little money and she just took a liking to him and got him straightened out, and...

Well, that's good. He was a good player. I liked him. He was one of them cats that I dug, man. He was all right. I guess they were all right in their way. But they still had that fence up, you know what I mean?
Yeah.

And I never will forget those cats, man, when Gene got busted, man... Nobody but me and Elton Hill was there, and everyone in that band split, man. We (?) to help pack the stuff up, you know. Damn shame, man. I guess (?) the spirit. I come from a different time. When bands were together, they were together. If it's a crisis, everybody stuck in there, you know what I mean?
Eldridge - 137
Yeah, that was sort of a mysterious thing that happened when he got busted. What was it they said? He sent the kid up, or...?

No, he didn't send him up. No, it wasn't like that at all. He didn't set him up. He was set up, really. You know, if he'd been smart... I told him, "Lay some bread on me, and I'll take the rap." Because they wanted a big cat. See, because this cat is running for District Attorney or something, and my name don't mean shit to them, you know what I mean. They know they ought not to do that, they ought not to go down to see the cat in the jail. And what happened is that they spent over a hundred thousand dollars, and they didn't have to spend that much with me, and would have been out scot-free, right? It's a real shame. It's a heartbreaking thing.
And you know, he did business... You wouldn't believe the business we did after that happened. After he came back, every place we played was like this.
But then he had to break up the band.

Yeah. I left the band for a while, because I couldn't stand those cats no more. All of a sudden, everybody was a star. We worked Atlantic City, Steel Pier, and we got through that all right. Then we went to... There's a ballroom, I don't know if it's called the
Eldridge - 138

Metropolitan Ballroom in Philadelphia. That's where I broke with the band. I couldn't make it. Every night, a different cat would pick me to follow me home. "How come you don't give me more solos?" I said, "You didn't play no more than that when Gene was here." Because I used to run the band when Gene was there, when he'd go out or something like that. I played the drums, too, you know. So I said, "Man, this ain't for me." No, it was too much, man.
Had Anita left by then?

Oh yeah, she'd been gone. Dolores Hawkins was there. And after Dolores left, there was another girl who joined. I think her old man used to play the saxophone or something. Gloria...Gloria...Gloria something. It wasn't Gloria Lynne; that's a Black singer.
Gloria Woods?
I don't know. I can't remember her last name. It was Gloria something. A brunette.
Did you meet Anita's book?
No.

She said some bad things about how you and she were the two big stars with Gene's band, there might have been some tension... You should read it, because I'm sure that what she says in there is not... It doesn't sound right to me.
I'm sure of that! I don't have it.
Eldridge - 139

It's a funny book. Aside from that, there's a lot of stuff in there that's quite interesting. She tells a lot of things about herself that you have to give her credit for talking about it the way she does. But there's a funny thing about you in there. She claims... She says that there was jealousy, you know.
Between me and her?
Yeah.

She's crazy. It must have been on her side! Heh-heh. First of all, I didn't think she could sing to start off with, so what am I gonna be jealous of? Oh, boy. I'll get her. Wait til I get to the Forties(?). Heh-heh, I'm glad you told me that.

No, there wasn't no jealousy on my part. Nope. Well, she forgets to mention she'd come down to the Deuces and sing, you know...
[END OF TAPE 3, SIDE 1]

I forgot to mention one of the greatest cats in there was Johnny Desmond. He was beautiful. And also Ray Everett. Those two cats I got along great with, you know, and there was no underhand things any kind of way. You see, I'm very sensitive to those things. You know, word gets
Eldridge - 140
around... See, a cat will laugh and grin with you, but then he'll make a mistake of saying something to other people, and then it gets back to you, you know. That's how I know.

Then I can tell by actions, too. Like, Ray would... If I had to stay across the tracks, he'd go and stay across the tracks with me. Nobody else would do that. Poor Ray died, too. I'm talking about Ray Biondi. That thing when Gene got arrested then... Well, Ray was in the middle of all that, you know. Ray was right there. Yeah, I liked that cat, man.

And Graham Young. He was here. He was right here before ...(?)... I knew his mother very well, because she used to always come by and see me. She was a nice lady. She played piano. He's doing very good, Graham Young. He's got him a nice boat, and his kids are all married. He's doin' real nice. I just got a call from him. He said him and his wife just climbed the Great Wall of China -- they were in China.
Oh yeah?
Yeah.
Was he lead trumpet?
No, Joe Giuscara(?) was lead. It was Joe, Ray, Graham and myself. He played lead on a lot of things. He was a good trumpet player. And he could play my things
Eldridge - 141
very good. He used to play... I have a... What did he used to play of mine? Oh, this arrangement they had on "Blues In The Night." He could really play the hell out of that.
Oh, another cat who used to be in that band I liked, too -- Norman Murphy. I just got a call from... You know, Norman had a heart attack, too.
Yeah, I heard.
He wrote me a letter, he said, 'It's not bad enough that I tried to play like you, but then I had to go and try to have a heart attack!' I owe him a letter. I've got to write him, too, you know.
[PAUSE]
So what happened after Gene?
After Gene, let's see... You mean after I broke with the band?
Yeah.

Then I went to... I started... After Gene I came back here, worked around here, and then... I think then I went in the studio with that Chesterfield show. And you know I didn't find out until later years that they had pickets on that show. Did you know that?
[SILENT]
Yeah, that's what I heard from a lot of sources. Because we had Teddy...
Eldridge - 142
That was CBS, wasn't it?

Yeah, the Chesterfield show. That was a farce, too, man! That's just one thing... I got out of there in a hurry, man. And also, the producer...in fact, he committed suicide. He was a good cat. Did you ever hear of a trumpet player named Lloyd Hundley? He was a good trumpet player. A Black cat. Some records are going to show up sooner or later with Shorty Sherock, myself, and Lloyd Hundley, and Tony DiAmore on piano. We played "The Sheik" and some other things, you know.
Were those regular records?
They were...
Transcriptions?
No, acetates. Acetates made in my house, you know.
Do you still have them?

Tony copied them. I don't know what happened to them after that. And somebody's liable to get them off him. Like they got some of the other things off him, you know. Charlie Graham Williams(?), he was (?) when he lost that tape that I made by myself with the five trumpets on it. I can't see how he could have did that. I can't see it.
Well, he gets so drunk.
He does?
Eldridge - 143
He probably recorded something over it or whatever he may have done...
You think he did that?
Yeah. He doesn't know from one moment to the next. But you know, the Chesterfield thing... Was Raymond Scott the bandleader in that?
No.
Paul Baron?
Paul Baron, yeah. He's out of the country now, you know. They ran him out, you know.
[PAUSE]
So where we at?
The Chesterfield show. That was kind of a breakthrough, wasn't it, because you were on staff, and...

Yeah. Supposed to be on staff. But you see what's wrong about that again? We were on staff, but we only had the one show. And the guys that we was working with, they had four or five different shows. It's really a farce, man, you know.
Listen. Did you ever hear that tape of "Four In The Bar"(?).
Mmm-hmm.
Well, did you notice how much I played on it, the Jazz I played on it? Everybody got a chance to play but
Eldridge - 144
me. Now, come on. Plus, on that same program...
[PAUSE FOR MOTOR NOISE]

If anybody was going to take a ballad on that thing, it should have been me, right? This is after I made "Rockin' Chair." It featured Jimmy Maxwell. He's a great trumpet player, but I mean, I think I should have done the ballad. But they featured him. And it was just like a... Well, it was just the wrong thing, man, you know. It was just like having a .400 hitter and you keep him on the bench.

And see, they never once had to stop for me to read the music, like what they did for those cats. That's another thing. I remember it took them quite some time to get through with that arrangement, you know. The only time they started with me at first was when they first ...(?)..., and he asked me to take a look at it. And I looked at it and I said, "Is it in one?" He said, "No." He said, "Well, take a look." I said, "Well, I'm looking. Is this the wrong key signature or what?" It was (?). It started out as a bugle like thing, you know, and when it come to my part, I didn't hear nobody playing the same thing I played. So I figured somebody wasn't reading, and I said, "Wait a minute! Somebody ain't readin'." Well, it lasted fifteen to twenty minutes. Then after I found out what was going on, it was a different thing, you know.
Eldridge - 145
And the only chance I had, man, was, oh, some chord changing here, and then back to the paper(?)...
Didn't you occasionally have a small group thing down there?
Not with me... Oh yeah! I don't think I got into that. Did you hear me playing on that?
I think there's one of "China Boy" or something...
It must have been Charlie Shavers.
No, it's you. But it's only about 16 bars or something.

I got out of there in a hurry, man. You know? Because what... So it's a big thing. So you're on staff. So what the hell does that mean? "Oh, yeah, I'm in the studio. I'm on staff." But if you ain't doin' nothin', hell, it ain't gonna mean nothin'. I'm not trying to impress nobody. I want to play.

Yeah, I'll (?) the same way I left Basie; you know, I went to Basie's band. Sit up there, doin' nothin' or... Hell, read music? I've been through that. I went over there because I thought I'd play some of them arrangements, you know, with Jo? Have some fun, you know. I didn't go over there to prove how much I could read. I did all of that!
Man, I very seldom got a chance to play with that band.
Eldridge - 146
At the end of the night, he'd play "After You've Gone" after I didn't play no Jazz all night long.
And you said they had pickets outside?

Yeah. I met Paul Baron in Rome. He was conducting a symphony in Rome, you know. And he said, "Well, they finally got me out of the country." This is going back a little bit, too. I said, "Yeah?" He said, "You know that show, when I hired you guys, Teddy and Al Hall..." Specs stayed on, because he got... He did get a break, because he got with this other cat, who was on The Ed Sullivan Show, Ray Brown. And Specs, Roy Eldridge, Al Hall, Teddy Wilson and Al Casey.
That's Specs Powell, right?
Yeah. So what had happened was that they were calling him a Communist for hiring a Black cat, you know. Then there were people picketing the place! -- which I never did know nothin' about that.
Who was picketing? Musicians?
Musicians, yeah. White musicians, what else?
So when you split from there, you started your own band again?
Let me see, did I start my own band again? I had a band in '43, didn't I. So it must have been there. That's when I started that band, yeah. The (?)Fish Market(?)
Eldridge - 147
band. Right, I had a big band there. I played around with that.
That was really big. I mean, that was bigger than what you had in the Arcadia band.
Oh yeah, that was a big band. I had three or four trombones, four trumpet, full reed section, guitar. Yeah.
Was Glaser still booking you then?
No.
