segments.title: Family origins, mother's piano and brother Joe
segments.summary: Roy gives his birth date and parents' origins, says he was the youngest of twelve, and credits his mother's piano playing and toy drums for his ear; Joe studied violin, harmony and arranging.

segments.title: Father's hauling and contracting business
segments.summary: Roy wanted to drive his father's trucks; he recalls the Model T touring car and cranking a truck into the garage wall.

segments.title: First paid job on drums at age six
segments.summary: Playing drums with Joe's violin, the Tatums and Norman Sampson at a wild private New Year's Eve party.

segments.title: Father's rooming house, shoeshine stand and business plans
segments.summary: His father tried to interest him in business with real estate, a rooming house, barbershop and shoeshine stand, which folded when Joe left.

segments.title: Piano lessons with a mean teacher
segments.summary: Roy quit piano after a teacher who slapped his hands frightened him.

segments.title: Drum lessons with Mr. Catlett and Joe's objection
segments.summary: He studied band drumming with Mr. Catlett (not related to Sid), but Joe said drums were too bulky to carry.

segments.title: Trumpet lessons with P.M. Williams
segments.summary: Joe got him a trumpet; P.M. Williams, a circus and carnival player, taught him, but Roy learned by ear and was not really reading, including a church duet.

segments.title: Drum-and-bugle corps and playing Taps
segments.summary: Joining a drum-and-bugle corps, loving parades, and the nervous first time he had to play Taps at the graveyard.

segments.title: Child in a stage play
segments.summary: A short memory of appearing as a child in a legitimate theatre play.

segments.title: Joe's band rehearsing at the family home
segments.summary: Joe's band, with Benny Carter at times, rehearsed at the house and then left for New York; Roy was still unsure about music.

segments.title: Rex Stewart as idol and learning off records
segments.summary: Roy and friends copied Red Nichols records; trumpeter Archie Johnson and Rex Stewart, who stayed at the house and showed him breaks, shaped him.

segments.title: Horace Henderson and the competitive spirit
segments.summary: Horace Henderson brought Roy into his band despite his not reading and told him stories of New York trumpet cutting contests.

segments.title: Local gigs with Chuck Jefferson
segments.summary: Playing basketball games and house parties in Homestead, staying out late and picking up money.

segments.title: Expelled from school and leaving for a road show
segments.summary: Roy was expelled after being caught with a white girl and left home on the day his father was to return him to school.

segments.title: First road show in Sharon, Pennsylvania
segments.summary: The band could not read the smeared music, the show was saved with a simple opener, and the stranded players gave ten-cent shows in a storefront.

segments.title: Youngstown dance and getting hired for a carnival
segments.summary: A five-dollar dance gig in Youngstown led to a party where Roy played Hawkins's Stampede chorus and was offered a job with a carnival band.

segments.title: Carnival band: hiding that he could not read
segments.summary: Roy struggled outdoors, was mocked by the piano players, was tricked into revealing he could not read, and ended up playing drums for the same twelve dollars.

segments.title: Seeing prejudice in Cumberland, Maryland
segments.summary: Describing the first time he saw violent racial prejudice, when the show owner struck a Black man and police jailed the Black men.

segments.title: Rock Dinah show and being cut by a singer
segments.summary: Roy fronted a road show band, was slashed with a razor by a singer, and refused to press charges against her.

segments.title: Meal tickets and the ice cream carton
segments.summary: On the road, Roy learned to grab food and filled a carton for later, learning in Kansas to reach for dishes.

segments.title: Roy Elliott and His Palais Royal Orchestra
segments.summary: As bandleader he was renamed Roy Elliott and featured East St. Louis Toodle-O with a gold tin can.

segments.title: Early influences: Fletcher, Red Nichols and Lips Page
segments.summary: Roy explains he sounded like Bix and a saxophone, and that Lips Page, meeting him in Oklahoma City, thought he played like a white man; he calls Louis-style playing Southern trumpet.

segments.title: Segregated theatres in his youth
segments.summary: Pittsburgh had integrated neighbourhoods but segregated theatres; the road showed him the real world.

segments.title: Bergie Hines's relatives' show in Oklahoma
segments.summary: Describing the road show in Oklahoma, a skit that had to be changed to a minstrel look, and the hostility to the pit band.

segments.title: Basie raiding his band in Kansas City
segments.summary: In Kansas City, Basie, then with Gonzelle White, took Roy's saxophonist Hildred Humphries and his banjoist; Roy explains how musicians were recruited.

segments.title: St. Louis trumpet players on Sundays
segments.summary: At a St. Louis hotel, Dewey Jackson, Baby James and others played Louis's Hot Five repertoire, which Roy found Southern and not his style.

segments.title: Hawkins, Carter, Buster Bailey and trouble with blues and ballads
segments.summary: Roy cites Coleman Hawkins, Benny Carter and Buster Bailey as models and says he could not play blues or ballads then.

segments.title: Tape change and the St. Louis hotel stay
segments.summary: Back to St. Louis: the trumpeters wiped him out every Sunday, and he lived in the hotel attic for weeks.

segments.title: Three carnivals and how they worked
segments.summary: After Rock Dinah he worked three carnivals with their own Pullman, privilege and gambling cars; musicians were nobodies.

segments.title: Quitting in Little Rock after a lynching
segments.summary: Roy quit the show after arriving in Little Rock a week after a man was lynched, and was threatened by a policeman.

segments.title: Big To-Do's band and Saturday parties in Mississippi
segments.summary: He played drums with Big To-Do's five-piece and at weekend parties with gambling behind a sheet while the show owner was away.

segments.title: Oliver Muldoon band and sending for his father
segments.summary: He joined the good but underemployed Oliver Muldoon band in Little Rock, then wired his father for help; his mother had died when he was ten.

segments.title: Jim Crow train and joy at the Pennsylvania train
segments.summary: On the journey home a conductor boasted about the Jim Crow car, and Roy wept with joy at seeing the Pennsylvania train.

segments.title: Back in Pittsburgh with Hen-Pie
segments.summary: Home around 1927, Roy worked with sax player Hen-Pie and joined Henderson.

segments.title: Horace Henderson's Stompers and the press roll
segments.summary: Describing the Horace Henderson band's name, book, personnel with Jonah Jones and Matthew Harlan, and his dislike of press rolls.

segments.title: Battle in Detroit and Joe telling him to learn to read
segments.summary: After winning a battle of music in Detroit Roy let it go to his head, and Joe made him quit Horace's band to learn to read.

segments.title: Detroit: the Chocolate Dandies jump band
segments.summary: Joe was with Earle Warren at the Majestic Ballroom; Roy joined a non-reading jump band under Jimmy Tisdale and recalls how well the musicians dressed.

segments.title: Battling the trumpeter Doll Jones
segments.summary: Roy describes meeting the woman trumpeter Doll Jones in a Detroit joint, who cut him until mid-afternoon, and lists other trumpeters there.

segments.title: Zack Whyte in Cincinnati and leaving over money
segments.summary: He stayed two weeks with Zack Whyte, with Sy Oliver as roommate, and left over leaders pleading poverty; his reputation was that he would not stay.

segments.title: Speed Webb's band
segments.summary: Speed Webb's band was as good as Lunceford's but never reached New York.

segments.title: Why he never learned to arrange
segments.summary: Roy had no eyes for arranging, writing only intros and a few bars, and reflects on being too busy playing.

segments.title: Picketing of the show with Teddy Wilson and Specs Powell
segments.summary: A recent gig featured five Black musicians with a thirteen-piece band while white musicians picketed.

segments.title: Lloyd Hundley, acetates and Tony's collection
segments.summary: Roy recalls trombonist Lloyd Hundley and acetates made at his house, and the pair worry about Tony's failing health and what happens to his collection.

segments.title: Speed Webb's band: arrangers and why it never came to New York
segments.summary: Speed Webb only fronted; the band included Gus Wilson, Teddy Wilson, Jonesy and others, wrote all night, never recorded, and the leader avoided New York.

segments.title: Battle of the bands in Flint with an old rival
segments.summary: Roy led the band, and the carnival pianist who had mocked him challenged him; the band beat him with classical arrangements and then a screamer.

segments.title: Band breaks up; Chinese restaurant job in Flint
segments.summary: After the band broke, Roy and Joe worked a restaurant job in Flint, and Roy fed the destitute former bandleader.

segments.title: Players he remembers, and Steve Dunn
segments.summary: Roy lists musicians he worked with, including Alvin Burroughs, Guy Jackson and trumpeter Steve Dunn of the Speed Webb band.

segments.title: Playing three sessions a day in the restaurant
segments.summary: The restaurant job meant playing light classical music at lunch and supper, and only dance music late.

segments.title: Run out of Flint, then Johnny Neal's band in Milwaukee
segments.summary: With Jonesy he stole wheels and fled Flint, then met Jabbo Smith while in Johnny Neal's band in Milwaukee.

segments.title: The radio incident that ended the Milwaukee job
segments.summary: Roy sang drunkenly on a radio broadcast, was cut off the air, and the manager paid him to leave town.

segments.title: Leaving for New York, and the childhood visit
segments.summary: He sold the car in Indianapolis, went home and then to New York, where he had first been as a kid around 1925-26.

segments.title: Minneapolis players and first meeting Art Tatum
segments.summary: He recalls Raymond Valentine and a Hines-like pianist in Minneapolis, and says he met Tatum when with McKinney's.

segments.title: From Cecil Scott and Smalls to the all-star Savoy band
segments.summary: Roy describes jobs in New York with Cecil Scott, Elmer Snowden and Charlie Johnson at Smalls, and an audition band with Cozy Cole, Kirby, Teddy Wilson and Chu Berry.

segments.title: New York musicians and being beaten down by Leonard Davis
segments.summary: The New York musicians' attitude scared him; Joe and Chu bought him gin and told him to stomp on the first trumpeter, and he never looked back.

segments.title: Meeting Louis at Smalls and the lip salve
segments.summary: Louis came to hear him at Smalls and called him Little Jazz; Roy's use of Louis's salve ruined his lips for a week.

segments.title: Hearing Louis at the Lafayette and becoming Little Jazz
segments.summary: Skeptical of the hype, Roy watched four shows, was floored by Louis's Chinatown, and learned it himself, winning a battle against Chick Webb.

segments.title: Charlie Johnson at Smalls and the film Smash Your Baggage
segments.summary: After Snowden's band folded Roy stayed with Charlie Johnson, and they discuss the film Smash Your Baggage.

segments.title: Smalls Paradise, John Hammond and Ed Small
segments.summary: Smalls was a black-and-tan place where he met Hammond; a rival's complaint about his Louis-style high notes led Ed Small to tell him to play himself.

segments.title: Absorbing Louis, Chick Webb's critique and ballads
segments.summary: Roy imitated Louis but kept to his own style; Chick Webb said he was fast but saying nothing, so he returned to Coleman's ballads.

segments.title: Leonard Feather misquoting him over Gene Krupa
segments.summary: Roy complains he was misquoted over his remarks about Gene hiring him and white bands.

segments.title: Vibrato and telling Black and white trumpeters apart
segments.summary: On returning from Europe he found everyone playing straight tone, so he could no longer tell Black from white players by vibrato.

segments.title: The 'No More White Bands for Roy' headline
segments.summary: A headline misrepresented his comment about having his own group, leading to attacks, with Zoot Sims and Phil Brown in the band.

segments.title: Greasy's and getting cut by Rex Stewart
segments.summary: After the Rhythm Club, Roy went with Rex Stewart to Greasy's on 129th, where Rex's high B-flat beat him.

segments.title: Working out the high B-flat
segments.summary: Roy woodshedded his range on China Boy and the next meeting ended in a standoff with Rex.

segments.title: A pest trumpet player in a red tux
segments.summary: A bad trumpeter in a red tux used to heckle Roy in New York.

segments.title: Playing with Art Tatum and his blindness
segments.summary: Roy took Tatum to the Rhythm Club, they jammed at the Devil's Kitchen, and Roy doubts Tatum was totally blind.

segments.title: Sorting out when he first knew Tatum
segments.summary: Roy tries to place when he met Tatum, Toledo, Cleveland or New York.

segments.title: Val's in the Alley jam sessions in Cleveland
segments.summary: With Prince Robinson, Joe, Clyde Hart and Lannie Scott, Roy jammed with Tatum in Cleveland during the hard Cotton Pickers days.

segments.title: Eldridge Brothers Rhythm Kings in Pittsburgh
segments.summary: After a wire warned him off New York Roy and Joe formed a Pittsburgh band with Kenny Clarke and beat local bands, then left for McKinney's.

segments.title: Joe looks out for him; Joe goes to California
segments.summary: Cotton Pickers folded, Joe, Prince and Clyde left for Blanche Calloway, and Joe preferred California to a gig Roy had.

segments.title: McKinney's breaks up; Teddy Hill and the Famous Door
segments.summary: McKinney's broke up in Baltimore, then he went to Teddy Hill, the Famous Door and Fletcher.

segments.title: Blowing his savings
segments.summary: Roy blew a week's savings treating friends and notes that he and Ben Webster were the only ones who saved.

segments.title: His group at the Famous Door
segments.summary: Roy led a group with Clyde Hart and Joe at the Famous Door, which kept them upstairs until the crowd left.

segments.title: Wingy Manone record date
segments.summary: On the Joe Marsala/Wingy Manone date, Wingy talked away the rest of the session; Roy recalls his first sight of him.

segments.title: Contact between Black and white musicians
segments.summary: He says musicians always got along; it was the other people.

segments.title: Big Matlock introduces him to Louis's records
segments.summary: In Omaha a Chicago musician played Louis records and introduced him to marijuana.

segments.title: Beau-Koo Jack, Teddy Wilson's arrangements and unused talent
segments.summary: They recall Roy and Jonah singing Beau-Koo Jack off Louis's record, and Teddy Wilson's scoring of Bix's solo.

segments.title: Wages and cheap suits in the 1930s
segments.summary: Roy made thirty-two dollars at the Savoy and bought cheap suits, noting how far money went.

segments.title: Famous Door again, Red Norvo and Joe Bushkin
segments.summary: After a tape change, Roy recalls the Famous Door arrangement of feeding the band upstairs, Red Norvo and young Joe Bushkin.

segments.title: Joining Fletcher Henderson
segments.summary: Having saved $500, Roy gambled it away in Philadelphia and then joined Fletcher, where Chu Berry had recommended him; the trumpet section included Thigpen.

segments.title: Breaking through on Fletcher's hard keys
segments.summary: Roy told Fletcher he could not play the hard keys but broke through at a Boston job.

segments.title: Going to Chicago with Fletcher, his marriage and the cold
segments.summary: He took seventy dollars, married the same day, and walked through frozen Chicago to rehearsal with Chu.

segments.title: Beating Earl Hines and the Christopher Columbus hit
segments.summary: The band outplayed Earl Hines at the Grand Terrace, made Christopher Columbus, and then publishing-driven arrangements led Roy to give notice.

segments.title: Leading the Three Deuces band with Zutty
segments.summary: Roy took a leader job at the Three Deuces with Zutty's group, added Joe, and the broadcast wire made the club a hangout.

segments.title: Sam Beers, Joe Glaser and hard times
segments.summary: His manager Sam Beers blocked a California offer and sold his contract to Joe Glaser; Roy pawned a ring to move the band.

segments.title: Decca date, pneumonia and Harold West on drums
segments.summary: Roy made a Decca session, caught pneumonia, and replaced Zutty with Harold West, who could not read.

segments.title: Meeting Jo Jones and Prez in Chicago
segments.summary: Roy befriended Prez and Jo Jones in Chicago, picking them up in his new Ford Roadster after work.

segments.title: Chicago after-hours clubs and Dorothy Donegan
segments.summary: Roy recalls Chicago clubs, breakfast dances, and Dorothy Donegan sitting in.

segments.title: Jamming with Tatum in Val's in the Alley
segments.summary: Roy recalls Tatum, Lannie Scott, and the jam sessions and broadcasts of the Cotton Pickers days.

segments.title: Dating when he knew Tatum
segments.summary: Discussing Adelaide Hall and trying to work out whether Tatum visited him at Smalls in 1931 or 1932.

segments.title: Recording with Tatum
segments.summary: Roy says Tatum accompanied well in clubs but took over the record date, and Moon Song recalled the Alley sessions.

segments.title: Lester Young's sound
segments.summary: Roy says Lester sounded when they first met as he did later.

segments.title: Giving up on tributes and TV shows
segments.summary: Roy says he is done with ceremonies after various mix-ups.

segments.title: Fletcher as bandleader and businessman
segments.summary: Roy discusses Fletcher's lack of business sense, recording deals for Moe Gale, Horace's role, and hard keys.

segments.title: Heckler's Hop and Gladys Palmer
segments.summary: Roy discusses the Heckler's Hop sides and Gladys Palmer's broadcasts.

segments.title: Leaving Chicago in 1938: Detroit and Cincinnati
segments.summary: On tour out of Chicago Roy recalls a debt dispute in Detroit and driving fast to the Cotton Club in Cincinnati.

segments.title: Zutty's temperament
segments.summary: Roy talks about Zutty's moods and habit of dropping the volume.

segments.title: The Tiger Rag standoff with Zutty at Terasi's
segments.summary: At Lew Terasi's patrons demanded Tiger Rag, Zutty sulked on the broadcast, and Roy left the stand and replaced him with Panama.

segments.title: Why he took the job and Zutty's playing
segments.summary: Roy explains he took the job after Zutty talked him into it, and Zutty played well on Louis's tunes.

segments.title: Teddy flips; Gabby joins on piano
segments.summary: After Teddy Wilson flipped, Roy hired Gabby and headed to Buckeye Lake.

segments.title: Mistaken arrest near Zanesville
segments.summary: A pianist robbed a post office and armed police detained the band at gunpoint until a boy identified him.

segments.chapter: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
segments.title: Return to the Savoy and meeting Joe Glaser
segments.summary: At the Savoy Roy hosted young trumpeters, and Glaser demanded he come to his office or not work.

segments.chapter: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
segments.title: Mal Hallett and union pressure
segments.summary: Playing at the Palace Theatre with Mal Hallett, who agreed to pay scale to protect him from Glaser's cut.

segments.chapter: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
segments.title: Glaser puts him in the Arcadia
segments.summary: Glaser's ten-piece stayed nine months at the Arcadia, and Roy had to pay for Don Redman's arrangements.

segments.chapter: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
segments.title: Playing tangos at the Arcadia
segments.summary: Roy had to learn dance music, got help from Paul Martell, and learned to play mellow dance sets.

segments.chapter: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
segments.title: Prince Robinson
segments.summary: Roy praises clarinetist Prince Robinson, who played the Albert system.

segments.chapter: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
segments.title: Golden Gate Ballroom and the pay dispute
segments.summary: At the Golden Gate with five bands, Roy waited for his pay in change.

segments.chapter: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
segments.title: Kelly's Stables
segments.summary: Roy led a small group at Kelly's Stables for several months, then Glaser sent him to Chicago.

segments.chapter: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
segments.title: Palm Garden in Milwaukee and a prejudiced owner
segments.summary: A prejudiced owner kept the band away from patrons until a friend threatened him.

segments.chapter: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
segments.title: Sunday sessions in Chicago and drinking zombies
segments.summary: Roy played Sunday gigs with Baby Dodds and Jimmy McPartland and drank zombies, and Shorty Sherock tried to get him drunk.

segments.title: Drumboogie and tunes he wrote for Gene
segments.summary: Roy composed tunes that Gene recorded, such as Drumboogie, without receiving royalties.

segments.title: Buying out his Glaser contract to join Krupa
segments.summary: Glaser let Frank Vernier buy his contract for a thousand dollars after Charlie Barnet balked.

segments.title: Joining Gene as an act and reading the book
segments.summary: At the Pennsylvania Hotel Roy shared the chair with Shorty Sherock, who was let go, and proved he could read.

segments.title: The Rockin' Chair story
segments.summary: Roy tells of the first time at Meadowbrook he split the high note and later redeemed it against Harry James at the Palladium.

segments.title: Relations with the band members
segments.summary: Only Ray Biondi and Graham Young were straight about race.

segments.title: Swing Is Here and the stolen melody
segments.summary: Roy's tune became Benny Goodman's, with Robbins publishing it and his manager Sam Beers threatening to sue.

segments.title: Radio engineering studies
segments.summary: Roy studied radio electronics before joining Glaser and by correspondence later, and notes that it became obsolete.

segments.title: Small talk about computers
segments.summary: A tangential chat about computers and word processors.

segments.title: Charlie Ventura in Gene's band
segments.summary: Roy recommended Ventura to Gene and kept him from quitting.

segments.title: Gene's bust and loyalty in the band
segments.summary: When Gene was arrested, only Roy and Elton Hill helped pack, and business boomed after he came back.

segments.title: Breaking with the band in Philadelphia
segments.summary: Roy left over the rivalry among sidemen at the Metropolitan Ballroom in Philadelphia.

segments.title: Anita O'Day and the vocalists
segments.summary: They discuss singers in the band and Anita O'Day's book, and Roy denies any jealousy.

segments.title: Johnny Desmond, Ray Biondi, Graham Young and the trumpet section
segments.summary: Roy fondly recalls band friends including Ray Biondi, Graham Young, Joe Giuscara and Norman Murphy.

segments.title: After Gene: the Chesterfield studio show
segments.summary: Roy joined the studio show, learned of the pickets, and calls it a farce.

segments.title: Acetates made at his house
segments.summary: Roy discusses the acetates with Shorty Sherock and Tony DiAmore and a lost tape.

segments.title: On staff with Chesterfield but never featured
segments.summary: Roy recalls that despite being on staff he got one show and almost no solos.

segments.title: Leaving the staff job; comparison with Basie
segments.summary: Roy left because staff status meant nothing without playing, as with Basie's band.

segments.title: Paul Baron on the picketing
segments.summary: Baron told Roy in Rome that he was called a Communist for hiring Black musicians.

segments.title: Forming his own big band
segments.summary: Roy had a big band in 1943 and no longer booked with Glaser.
